subject: physics

items.q: Which statement describes nuclear fission?
items.correct: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus such as a uranium nucleus.
items.misconception: The joining of two light nuclei into a single heavier nucleus.
items.why: The words look and sound alike, both begin with 'f', and both are met in the same short section of the course. Fission has the sense of a fissure, a split. Fusion has the sense of fusing, of joining. Fission needs a large unstable nucleus; fusion needs two light ones.
items.random_wrong: The breaking of a nucleus into its separate protons and neutrons.

items.q: A power station uses uranium as its fuel. Why can a uranium nucleus undergo fission when a carbon nucleus cannot?
items.correct: A uranium nucleus is large and unstable, so it can split.
items.misconception: A carbon nucleus can be split just as easily as a uranium one.
items.why: The phrase 'splitting the atom' is used loosely in everyday language, so students assume it applies to atoms in general. Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus. Small stable nuclei such as carbon do not undergo fission.
items.random_wrong: A uranium atom holds more electrons than a carbon atom.

items.q: Spontaneous fission is rare. What must usually happen before a large unstable nucleus undergoes fission?
items.correct: The unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
items.misconception: The unstable nucleus must be heated to a high temperature.
items.why: Students have heard that fusion needs extremely high temperatures and transfer that condition across to fission, helped by knowing that a reactor core is hot. Fission is triggered by the nucleus absorbing a neutron, not by heating. The reactor is hot because fission releases energy, not the other way round.
items.random_wrong: The unstable nucleus must first absorb a proton.

items.q: A uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission. Apart from gamma rays, what does the fission produce?
items.correct: Two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, plus two or three neutrons.
items.misconception: Two smaller nuclei of about the same size, and a single extra neutron.
items.why: Students reason that one neutron goes in, so one neutron must come out, and one is all that is needed to keep the process going. Two or three neutrons are emitted. That is why the reaction can grow: more neutrons come out than went in.
items.random_wrong: One large nucleus and one very small nucleus, plus a few free neutrons.

items.q: A uranium nucleus undergoes fission. Which statement about the two nuclei it produces is correct?
items.correct: They are roughly equal in size, and both are smaller than the uranium nucleus.
items.misconception: They are stable, so no further radiation is ever emitted by them.
items.why: Students assume that splitting solves the instability, so the products must be finished with radioactivity. The two smaller nuclei are still unstable, which is why spent fuel from a reactor stays radioactive for a long time.
items.random_wrong: One is much larger than the other, and the smaller is a proton.

items.q: In a fission event, which of the products are given kinetic energy?
items.correct: All of them, including each of the neutrons that are emitted.
items.misconception: Only the two smaller nuclei that are formed by the split.
items.why: Diagrams often show the two nuclei being pushed apart, so students give the energy to those and treat the neutrons as passengers. All of the fission products have kinetic energy, the neutrons included. Fast-moving neutrons are what allows a chain reaction to spread.
items.random_wrong: None of them, since the energy is carried off by the gamma rays.

items.q: Why can a single fission event lead to a chain reaction?
items.correct: The neutrons released are absorbed by other nuclei, making those split too.
items.misconception: The gamma rays given out are absorbed by other nuclei, making those split too.
items.why: Gamma rays are named in the list of products and are known to be penetrating, so students assume they are the active agent. The neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction. Gamma rays are emitted, but it is the absorbed neutrons that trigger further fission.
items.random_wrong: The energy released heats the fuel up until the nuclei around it break apart.

items.q: How does the chain reaction inside a nuclear reactor differ from the one in a nuclear weapon?
items.correct: In the reactor it is controlled; in the weapon it is not.
items.misconception: The reactor releases energy slowly because it uses a different fuel.
items.why: Students look for a difference in the material rather than in how the reaction is managed, because materials are the usual explanation in chemistry. The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released. The weapon's explosion is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.
items.random_wrong: The reactor splits nuclei, while the weapon works by joining them.

items.q: The chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is controlled. What does controlling it achieve?
items.correct: It keeps the rate of fission steady, so the energy is released steadily.
items.misconception: It stops the chain reaction, so that no further fission takes place.
items.why: Both are described as 'nuclear', and news coverage blurs the difference between a release of radioactive material and a nuclear explosion. The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor so that the energy released stays steady. Only the weapon uses an uncontrolled chain reaction.
items.random_wrong: It makes the reaction spread faster, so more energy is given out.

items.q: A student is drawing a chain reaction diagram. One neutron causes a fission that releases three neutrons, and each of those is absorbed by another uranium nucleus. What should the diagram show next?
items.correct: Three further fissions, each of them releasing three more neutrons.
items.misconception: One further fission, with the two spare neutrons simply stopping there.
items.why: The word 'chain' suggests a line of single links, and drawing one fission after another is simpler than drawing a branching tree. Each released neutron can cause a further fission, so the diagram branches: one fission, then three, then nine. That growth is what makes the reaction spread.
items.random_wrong: Three further fissions, each of them releasing one new neutron.

items.q: Which statement describes nuclear fusion?
items.correct: Two light nuclei join to form a single heavier nucleus.
items.misconception: Two heavy nuclei join together to form one lighter nucleus.
items.why: Students remember 'joining nuclei' without the condition on their size, and uranium is the nucleus they have most recently met. Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. Heavy nuclei such as uranium are the fuel for fission, not fusion.
items.random_wrong: A large unstable nucleus splits into two fragments.

items.q: Two light nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus. What may happen to some of their mass?
items.correct: It is converted into the energy of radiation.
items.misconception: It is thrown out of the new nucleus as extra neutrons.
items.why: Students assume that mass can only be accounted for by more matter, so they invent particles to carry it away. In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation. The mass is not relocated into other particles; it becomes energy.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, since mass is always conserved.

items.q: When a large nucleus undergoes fission, what does it break into?
items.correct: Two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, together with two or three neutrons and gamma rays.
items.misconception: The nucleus comes apart into all of its separate protons and neutrons.
items.why: Students picture the nucleus as a loose bag of particles, so 'splitting' suggests the bag bursting and every particle spilling out. The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei. Each of those is still a nucleus holding many protons and neutrons together; only two or three single neutrons are emitted.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which particle must the unstable nucleus absorb for fission to occur?
items.correct: A neutron.
items.misconception: The nucleus has to absorb a proton, an alpha particle or a gamma ray.
items.why: Students remember that 'something goes in' but not what. A charged proton or alpha particle feels like a harder hit, so it seems more likely to break the nucleus. The specification is specific: for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. Neutrons are uncharged, so they are not repelled by the nucleus.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the sizes of the two nuclei produced by fission?
items.correct: They are roughly equal in size.
items.misconception: Fission chips a tiny fragment off the nucleus, leaving one large nucleus and one very small one.
items.why: Students carry over the picture of alpha decay, where a large nucleus emits a small alpha particle and stays almost the same size. In fission the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei that are roughly equal in size. Emitting a small fragment is radioactive decay, not fission.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which of the fission products have kinetic energy?
items.correct: All of them.
items.misconception: The energy released is carried away only as gamma radiation, so the particles produced are left almost at rest.
items.why: Gamma rays are the most obviously 'energetic' item in the list of products, so students assume they carry all of the energy released. All of the fission products have kinetic energy. Gamma rays are emitted as well, but the nuclei and the neutrons are moving fast too.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does one fission lead to further fissions?
items.correct: The neutrons it releases can be absorbed by other unstable nuclei.
items.misconception: The energy released heats the fuel, and the heat makes the neighbouring nuclei break apart.
items.why: Students transfer everyday ideas about heat spreading through a material, and they know that reactors get hot. The chain reaction is spread by neutrons being absorbed, not by heating. Temperature does not decide whether a nucleus undergoes fission.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the mass in a fusion reaction?
items.correct: Some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
items.misconception: The total mass cannot change, because mass is always conserved.
items.why: Conservation of mass is drilled thoroughly in chemistry, so students apply it to a nuclear change in which some mass is converted into energy. In fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus has less mass than the two light nuclei had.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which part of the atom changes in nuclear fission?
items.correct: The nucleus. It splits into two smaller nuclei.
items.misconception: Fission is about the electrons: the atom is split by knocking electrons off it.
items.why: The only 'splitting' students have met before is ionisation or bond breaking, and both of those really do involve electrons. Fission is a nuclear change. The nucleus itself splits; the electrons play no part in whether fission happens.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is fusion the same as two atoms bonding together?
items.correct: No. Fusion joins two nuclei to form a single heavier nucleus.
items.misconception: Fusion means atoms joining to make a molecule or a compound.
items.why: 'Joining together' is exactly how chemical bonding is described, so students reach for the chemistry they already know. Fusion is a nuclear process: the two nuclei themselves merge into one heavier nucleus. Bonding leaves both nuclei completely unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
